components.gap: Preserve the justificatory principle Durrett gives for the truncation level in Example 2.2.16 (Version 5, p. 65): in checking condition (ii) of Theorem 2.2.11 one wants b_n as small as possible while condition (i) still holds; this is what guides the choice b_n = 2^(m(n)) with m(n) = log_2 n + K(n) and K(n) tending to infinity. The entry states the choice without this rationale.

components.gap: Preserve the normative and historical claims of the source presentations of the meaning of the scale. Durrett Example 2.2.16 (Version 5, pp. 65-66): the paradox that E X_1 is infinite although one clearly would not pay an infinite amount to play; that Theorem 2.2.11 tells how much one should pay to play n times; that a fair price for playing n times is log_2 n per play (10 dollars per play at n = 1024); Nicolas Bernoulli's 1713 statement that any halfway sensible person would sell the right to play for 40 ducats per play; and the remark that about 2^40, roughly 10^12, plays would be needed to start to break even. The entry gives the numbers 10 and 2^40 only as asymptotic scale calculations and says they specify no break-even probability, without reporting the source's fair-price, Bernoulli and break-even claims. Feller Vol. II, VII.7 (p. 236): the fair-game framing preceding Theorem 2 (even when expectations exist a participant in a fair game may be strongly on the losing side; the St. Petersburg analysis shows the classical theory applies to certain games with infinite expectation except that the fair entrance fee depends on the contemplated number of trials, which Theorem 2 makes precise) and the interpretation of X_k as possible gains and a_n as the total entrance fee for n trials.
